speeches.Boye:: Here ſit! Oh like hops and harlots ſir!
speeches.Mi:: Lay by my conſcience, giue mee my Gowne, That weede is for the country, We muſt be ciuill now, and match out Euill, Who firſt made Ciuill, blacke; he pleas'd the Deuill; So; now know I where I am, me thinkes already I graſpe beſt part of the Autumnian bleſſing In my contentious fadome, my hand's free, From wronger and from wronged I haue fee, And what by ſweat from the rough earth they drawe, Is to enrich this ſiluer harueſt, Lawe, And ſo through wealthy variance, and fat brawle, The Barne is made but Steward to the Hall; Come they vp thicke inough? Why do'ſt thou couple them? Such another and bee my heyre, I haue no Childe, Yet haue I wealth would redeeme beggery, I thinke it be a curſe both here and forraine, Where bags are fruitful'ſt, there the womb's moſt barren, The poore ha's all our children, we their wealth; Shall I be prodigall when my life cooles, Make thoſe my heyres whome I haue beggar'd; Fooles? It would be wondrous; rather beggar more, Thou ſhalt haue heyres enow, thou keep'ſt a whore, And here comes kindred too with no meane purſes, Yet ſtriue to be ſtill bleſt with Clients curſes. What ſubtiltie haue we here? a fellowe Shrugging for lifes kind benefits, ſhift and heate, Crept vp in 3. Termes, wrapt in ſilke and ſiluer, So well appointed too with Page and Pandar, It was a happy gale that blew him hether. Your dutie and regard hath mou'd vs, Neuer till now wee thought you lou'd vs, Take comfort from our words, and make no doubt, You ſhall haue ſuites come ſixteen times about. With what a vaſſaile—appetite they Gnawe, On our reuerſions; and are proud, Coldly to taſt our meates, which eight returnes Serue in to vs as courſes; One day our writs like wilde-fowle flye abroad, And then returne or'e Cities, Townes, and Hills, With Clyents like dryed ſtrawes betweene their bills; And 'tis no few birds picke to build their Neaſts, Nor no ſmall money that keeps Drabs and Feaſts!
speeches.Boy:: Oh very aptlye, for as the hop well boiled will make a man not ſtand vppon his leggs: ſo the harlot in time will leaue a man no leggs to ſtand vppon!
We humbly thanke the patron of our hopes. Agreed.
speeches.Rer:: Maſter Salewood ▪ Exceedingly well met in Towne, comes your Father vp this Terme? But will ſhee paſſe ſo thinke you? They're worthy ſpirits yfaith, heard you the Newes? Miſtris Difficult is falne a widdowe. Eaſilie dead ſir. What a queſtion's that? when ſhould a Lawyer dye but in the vacation, hee ha's no leiſure to die in the Tearme time, beſide the Noyſe there would fetch him againe. Faith ſome ſay he dyed of an old griefe he had, that the vacation was foureteene weekes long. He ſauours, ſtop your Noſe, no more of him. What gentleman might that bee? Faith ſir, I am vildly riuald! One Andrewe Lethe crept to a little warmth, and now ſo proud that he forgets all ſtormes, one that nere wore apparell, but like ditches 'twas caſt before hee had it, now ſhines bright in rich embroderies, him maſter Quomodo af fects, the daughter him, the mother onely mee, I reſt moſt doubtfull, my ſide being wookeſt. Slid maſter Quomodo? He warn'd mee his houſe, and I hate hee ſhould ſee me abroad! No, Andro Lethe! Has forgot his fathers name, poore Walter Gruill that begot him, fed him, and brought him vp. No; 'twas from his thoughts, hee brought him vp belowe. Mongſt ſtrange eyes that no more knowe him, then he knowes him ſelfe, thats nothing now, for maſter Andro Lethe, a gentleman of moſt receiued parts, forgetfulnes, Luſt, Impudence, and Falſhood, and one eſpeci all Courtly quality; to wit, no wit at all, I am his Riuall for Quomodoes daughter, but hee knowes it not. Oh thats a warning to make our duties ready. Puh, wiſh his health a while, heele be laide ſhortly, let him gorge Veniſon for a time, our doctors will bring him to dry mutton; ſeeme reſpectiue to make his pride ſwell like a Toade with dewe. Sweete maſter Lethe. Caſt it. Gentlemen I ha ſworne Ile change the roome: dice?
Why he was here three dayes before the Exchequer gapte. Hee's not to bee ſpoke withall, I dare not aske him bleſſing, till the laſt of Nouember. Faith like a Lute that ha's all the ſtringes broke, no bodie will meddle with her. Sh' as no lucke, ſome may better ſteale a horſe than others looke on. I haue knowen a virgin of fiue baſtardes wedded, faith when all's donne we muſt bee faine to marrie her into the North I'me affrayd. Heere's lucke. Ile bee damn'd and theſe bee not the bones of ſome queane that couzened me in her life, and now conſumes mee after her death. Why, what's the matter?
Fye, ſuch an earlie Termer? And how looks thy little venturing Cooſen? Fye, there are Doctors enow in Towne will ſtring her againe, and make her ſound as ſweete as ere ſhee did, is ſhee not married yet? Nay come, will ye draw in Gentlemen? ſet me: The Diuell and his Angels. Oh worſe then conſumption of the Liuer! conſump tion of the patrimonie. Forgiue me, my poſte • itie, yet vngotten. Few knowe the ſweets that the plaine life allowes. Vilde ſonne that ſurfets of his fathers browes. Tennants! When's our next meeting Gentlemen? And that's a Villanous torment. And not for loue? this makes for me his Riuall, beare witneſſe. And ene now he cald me by it. Firſt as a contempt of that reuerend Ceremony, hee has in hand, to wit, marriage. And ſo the wa • ch that ſhould fe • ch her out ▪ are her chiefeſt guard to keepeher in. Why well then. We were all three in a minde then. I wonder he keepes ſo long from vs yfaith. I wo ̄ der you ſhuld miſſe on't lately, you'r his bedfelow Content yfaith, let's trace him. I entertaine both thee and thy Deuice, Twill put e'm both to ſhame. Saue you ſweete widdowe, I ſuffer for your heauineſſe. Yet if all tongues goe right, hee did not vſe you ſo wel as a man mought. Why I count you the wiſer Widdowe, it ſhowes you haue wiſdome, when you can checke your paſſion, for mine owne part, I haue no ſence to ſorrowe for his death, whoſe life was the onely Rub to my affection. But Lethe lyes'ith way. Sweete widdowe. Here they come. There goes the ſtrumpet. I doe embrace thee in the beſt of loue, How ſoone affections fail, how ſoone they proue. His owne Mother my Lord, Which hee confeſt through ignorance, and diſdaine, His name ſo chang'd to abuſe the world and her.
speeches.Sal:: Puh, any thinge that is warme ynough is good y nough for them; ſo it come in the likenes, tho the Deuill be in't, the'ile venture the fiering. Not yet. Say true, is Maſter Difficult the Lawyer dead? Pray when died hee? Knew you the nature of his diſeaſe. And very likely. I knew 'twould kill him at laſt, t'as troubled him a long time, hee was one of thoſe that would faine haue brought in the hereſie of a fift Tearme, often cry ing with a loud voice, oh why ſhould we looſe Bartholmew weeke?
speeches.Cock:: Yong maiſter Eaſye, let me ſalute you ſir, when came you? You ſeldome viſit London maſter Eaſye, But now your Fathers dead tis your onely courſe, Here's gallants of all ſizes, of all laſts, Here you may fit your foote, make choyſe of thoſe Whome your affection may reioyce in: Maſter Rerrage? One maſter Eſay, h'as good • nd in Eſſex, a faire free-breſted Gentleman, ſomewhat too open, bad in man, worſe in woman, the Gentrye-fault at firſt, he is yet freſh and wants the Citie powdring, but what newes? I'ſt yet a match twixt maſter Qomodoes the rich Drapers daughter and your ſelfe. Vildly? by whome. Yet the mothers ſide being ſurer than the Fathers, it may proue, men pleade for money beſt, women for loue. How then, affraid of a woollen draper. What newes in yonder paper. Salute him, hang him. Taſt it. Firſt dogs take paines to make it fit for men, Then men take payne to make it fit for dogs. Why this is kindnes, a kind Gallant, you, And loue to giue the dogs more than their due, We ſhall attend you ſir.
speeches.Eaſye:: I haue but Inn'd my horſe ſince maſter Cockstone. You haue eaſily poſſeſt me I am free, Let thoſe liue hindes that know not libertie. What's here?
speeches.Eaſ:: Good maſter Salewood, I am proud of your ſociety. Againſt Saint Andrewes, at a Painters houſe, ther's a faire chamber ready furniſht to bee let, the houſe not onely endewed with a newe faſhion forepart, but which is more conuenient for a Gentleman, with a very prouident backe-doore. Hees ſecond to my boſome. No ſir? Then I deſire to be more deere vnto you. I count my ſelfe the happier. The Deuill grinde thy Bones, thou co • ſning Raſ cal.
speeches.Quo:: Oh my 2. ſpirits Shortyard and Falſelight, you that haue ſo enricht me, I haue induſtrie for you both? Wealthy employment. You Falſelight as I haue directed you. Goe, make my courſe commodities, looke, ſeeke, with ſubtile art beguile the honeſt eye, be neere to my trap windowe, cunning Falſelight. I know thou didſt not; But now to thee my true and ſecret Shortyard, Whome I dare truſtee'n with my wife, Thou nere didſt miſtris harme, but maſter, good, There are too few of thy name Gentlemen, And that we feele, but Citizens abundance, I haue a taske for thee my pregnant ſpirit, To exerciſe thy poynted wits vppon. Thine care ſhall drinke it, Know then I haue not ſpent this long Vacation Onely for pleaſures ſake, giue me the man Who out of recreation culls aduantage, Diues into ſeaſons, neuer walkes, but thinkes, Ne • ides, but plots, my iourney was toward Eſſex. Where I haue ſeene what I deſire. Puh; a woman, yet beneath her, that which ſhee often treades on. Yet commands her land, fayre neate Land. Why the fayreſt to cleaue the heire in twayne, I meane his Title to murder his eſtate, ſtifle his right in ſome ſome deteſted priſon, there are means and waies enow to hooke in Gentry, be ſides our deadlye enmitye which thus ſtands they'r buſye 'bout our wiues, We 'bout their Lands. Ah ſirrah, doe we ſtinge'm, this freſh gallant rode newly vp before me! Yong maſter Eaſye. I haue enquir'd his haunt, ſtay, ha, I that, 'tis, thats he, thats he! Obſerue, take ſurely note of him, hee's freſh and free ſhift thy ſelfe ſpeedily into the ſhape of gallan trye, Ile ſwell thy purſe with angels, keepe foote by foote with him, out-dare his expences, flat ter, dice, and brothell to him, giue him a ſweete taſt of Senſuality, traine him to euery waſtfull ſin, that he may quickly neede health, but eſpecially money, rauiſh him with a dame or twoo, bee his bawde for once, Ile bee thine for euer, drinke drunke with him, creepe into bed to him, kiſſe him and vndoo him, my ſweete ſpirit. O my moſt cherefull ſpirit, goe, diſpatch, Gentrye is the cheife fiſh we Tradeſmen catch.
speeches.Sho:: Then doe you pleaſe vs beſt ſir. You make me icth ſir. Moſt true? A woman? What is the marke you ſhoote at. Your reuenge is more glorious, To be a cuckold is but for one life, When land remaines to you, your heire, or wife! I beſeech his name. Eaſye? It may fall right. Happilie! Let your care dwell in me ſoone ſhall it ſhine, What ſubtiltie is in man, that is not mine. An Essex genrleman ſir. Indeed ſir. Ile giue you that comfort then ſir, you muſt not want money as long as you are in towne ſir. I am bound in my loue to him to ſee you furniſht, and in that comfort I recouer my ſalute agen ſir. I rather ſtudy to be deare vnto you—boy, fill ſome wine.—I knew not what faire impreſſier I receiud, at firſt, but I began to affect your ſocietie very ſpeedily. To maſter Alſup ſir, to whoſe remembrance, I could loue to drinke till I were paſt remembrance. How now Boy?
speeches.Falſ:: I am nimble. I neuer failde it yet.
Giue it me, for I thirſt. Your ſuite ſhall end in one Tearme ſir: my name is Blaſtfield. Sir, you ſhall not giue out ſo meanely of your ſelfe in my companie for a Million: make Such priuie to your diſ grace? you'r a Gentleman of faire fortunes; keep me your re putation; ſet 'em all, there's crownes fo you. You muſt alwayes haue a care of your Reputation here in Town maiſter Eaſie, altho you ride downe with no thing, it skils not. Why, well ſaid. And then you'le leaue vs, thats your faſhion. But hee's more baſe taht carries out his winnings. None will doe ſo but thoſe haue baſe beginnings I wonder you ſhould paſſe. And that you're ſufferd. I knew the time, he wore not halfe a ſhirt, iuſt like a Pee. Faith he compounded with a couple of Napkins at Barnet, and ſo truſ'd vp the lower parts. But maiſter Lethe ha's forgot that too. Nay but good Ma Eaſie, do not do your ſelf that tiran nie I beſeech you, I muſt not ha you alter your body now for the Purge of a little money: you vndoe me and you doe. Pox of money, talke not on't I beſeech you, what ſaid I to you? Maſſe I am out of caſh my ſelfe too,—Boy. Run preſently to maſter Gum the Mercer, and wil him to tell out two or three hundred pound for mee, or more ac cording as he is furniſht: Ile viſit him ith morning ſay. Doe you heare boy? If maſter Gum bee not ſufficiently readie, call vppon maſter Profit the Goldſmith. Boy. Let them both reſt till another occaſion: you ſhall not need to run ſo farre at this time, take one nier hand go to Ma. Quomodo the Draper, and will him to furniſh mee inſtantly. Maſter Eaſie, let a man beare himſelfe portly, the whor ſons will creepe to him a'th their bellies, and their wiues a'th their backs: ther's a kinde of bolde grace expected through out all the parts of a Gentleman: then for your obſeruances, a man muſt not ſo much as ſpit but within line and faſhion. I tell you what I ha done: ſomtimes I carrie my water all Lon don ouer, onely to deliuer it proudly at the Standard, and do I paſſe altogether vnnoted thinke you? No, a man can no ſooner peep out his head, but ther's a bow bent at him out of ſome watch tower, or other. Puſh, you know a bowe's quickely readie, tho a Gun belong a charging, and will ſhoote fiue times to his once, Come, you ſhall beare your ſelfe Iouially: take heede of ſetting your lookes to your loſſes, but rather ſmile vppon your ill lucke, and inuite 'em to morrow to another breake faſt of Bones. What? peace? I am aſhamed to heare you: will you ceaſſe in the firſt loſſe, ſhewe mee one Gentleman that ere did it? Fie vppon't I muſt vſe you to companie I perceyue, youde be ſpoilde elſe: forſweare Dice? I would your friends heard you yfaith. I hope ſo, what woulde Gentlemen ſay of you? there goes a Gull that keepes his money, I would not haue ſuch a report goe on you, for the Worlde as long as you are in my companie. Why man fortune alters in a Minute, I ha knowne thoſe haue recouered ſo much in an houre, their purſes were neuer ſicke after. How now? marke their humours maſter Eaſie. Thats a penitent Maudlen Dicer. Laugh at him maſter Eaſie. Thats the true-wicked-blaſphemous, and ſoul-ſhud dering Dicer, that will curſe you all ſeruice time, & attribute his ill lucke alwayes to one Drab or other. Why, we thanke him yfaith. Not ſo I beſeech you, I giue my friends leaue to bee inward with me,—will you walke Gentlemen? What good ſweete bedfellow. Maſſe that was well remembred of thee—I per ceyue the Trout will bee a little troubleſome ere hee bee catcht—Boy. 〈…〉 Boy ▪ Here ſir. Runne to Maſter Goome, or Maſter Profite, and car rie my preſent occaſion of money to em. Why maiſter Quomodo, what a fruitleſſe Motion haue you put forth, you might wel • aſſure your ſelfe this gen tleman had it not if I wanted it: why our purſes are brothers we deſire but equall fortunes: in a word w'are man and wife, they can but lie together, and ſo doe we. And to ſay truth, tis more for the continuing of this Gentlemans credit in Towne then any incitement from mine owne want only, that I cou • t to be ſo immediatly furniſh • — you ſhall heare him confeſſe as much himſelfe. Oh here comes the Boy now: How now Boy, what ſayes maiſter Goome, or maſter Profit? A Baſtard be it, ſpite and ſhame. Bewitcht I thinke. So diſaſtrouſly. The mealie Moth conſume it, would hee hame turne Pedler now? what ſhould I doe with cloath? And thy vtter diſſolution amongeſt Gentlemen for e •• er. Quomodo ſhould hang, rot, ſtinke. Drop Dam. Maiſter Richard Eaſie: you may eaſily hit on't. I neuer paſſe my Month you know. I neuer miſſe you. Puſh, their ordaind to ſweate for Gentlemen,— Porters backes and womens bellies beare vp the world. Ye'aue found it ſir. Come Maſter Eaſie. It ſhall be yours I ſay. I will not yfaith. I ſhould ſhew little bringing vp, to take the way of a ſtranger. Not a whit ſir. Let it be ſo I pray. So his right wing is cut, will not flie farre Paſt the two Cittie hazards, Poultrie, and Woodſtreete. We doe ſir. Would the Coyne would come away now, we haue deſeru'd for't How now? what's the matter? ſpeake? What's the newes? Piſh— Why what would you ſay? I where? how? the beſt is it lyes all vppon my necke, Maiſter Quomodo, can you help me to any money fort? ſpeak His name: Sfoo't will he giue any thing. Will he giue any thing?—the Brokers will giue no thing? to no purpoſe. What if hee ſhould offer but a hundred pound? Say you ſo? Tis true, he ſaide ſo indeede. For indeede he ha's no grace at all. This ſir, but I ſcarce like my Miſtris now: the loynes can nere be ſafe where the Flyes be ſo buſie— Witte by experience bought foyles wit at Schoole: Who proues a deeper knaue then a Spent foole, I am gone for your worſhips wine ſir. Yet at laſt, Maiſter Quomodo is as firme as his promiſe. Let me ſee, I am ſeauen hundred pound in bond now to the Raſcall. That's my Ambition ſir. Is that the beauty you famde ſo? Who be thoſe ſo induſtrious about her? Prethee whats that? Ha they ſo little conſcience? You parcell of a rude, ſawcie and vnmannerly nation. Cannot a Gentleman purchaſe a little fire to thawe his appetite by, but muſt you that haue beene dayly ſindg'd in the flame, be as greedy to beguile him on't? how can it ap peare in you but maliciouſly, and that you goe about to en groſſe hell to your ſelues? he auen forbid, that you ſhould not ſuffer a ſtranger to come in, the Deuill himſelfe is not ſo vn mannerly, I doe not thinke but ſome of them rather will be wiſe enough to beg ▪ Offices there before you, and keepe you out, marry all the ſpite will bee they cannot ſell e'm a gen. Clubs, clubs,—Gentlemen ſtand vppon your Guard. And to conclude a Coward, infallible of your ſide, why doe you thinke yfaith I tooke you to be a Coward? doe I thinke youle turne your backe to anye man liuing? youle be whipt firſt. But that man ſhowes himſelfe a Knaue, for he dares not ſhowe his owne face when hee does it, for ſome of the common Counſell in Henry the eights daies thought it mo deſtie at that time, that one Vizzard ſhould looke vppon a nother. How now? what peece of ſtuffe comes heere? Vinited. Toe's all To ſweete Maiſter Lethe. This Re • iſh wine is like the ſcowring-ſticke to a gun, it makes the Barrell cleere: it ha's an excelent vertue, it keepes all the Sinckes in man and womans bodie ſweete in Iune and Iuly, and to ſay truth, if Ditches were not caſt once a yeare, and Drabs once a Month, there would be no abiding i'th Cittie. A letter comes well after priuie, it makes amends. Are you not well? Birlady and the Mother is a peſtilent, wilfull, trouble ſome ſickneſſe I can tell you, if ſhe light vpon you handſom lye. Very aſſuredly. Did you let it goe ſo yfaith? I, her anſwere. Nay, heare out hir anſwere, or there's no goodneſſe in you. Show your ſelfe a Gentleman, ſhe had the patience to reade your letter which was as bad as this can be, what will ſhe thinke on't, not heare her anſwere? ſpeake, good his drudge. That's verie wholſome for your body, nay you muſt keepe in your armes. And you loue me, lets follow him Gentlemen. I count a hundred pound wel ſpent to perſue a good ieſt Maiſter Eaſie. Well ſaide yfaith, hang money-good ieſts are worth ſiluer at all times. So, No man is ſo impudent to denye that— Spirits can change their ſhapes, and ſooneſt of all into Serjeants: becauſe they are Cooſen Germans to ſpirits, for there's but two kinde of arreſts till Doomeſ-day, the Deuill for the ſoule, the Serjeant for the body, but afterward the de uill arreſts bodye and ſoule Serjeant & all, if they be knaues ſtill, and deſerue it ▪ now my yeoman • aſlight. Neuer let •• come neere thy belee • e that heele take pri ſon, or ſtand out in lawe, knowing the debt to be due, but ſtill expect the preſence of Maiſter Blaſtfield, kinde M. Blaſt field, worſhipfull M Blaſtfield—and at the laſt— The Boy: a warning-piece,—ſee where he comes. Maiſter Richard Eaſie of Eſſex we arreſt you. Deliuer your weapons quietly ſir. Y'are arreſted at the ſuite of M. Quomodo. How ſtrange you make it, you'r a landed Gentleman ſir, I knew tis but a triſſe, a bond of ſeauen hundred pound. Is not your name there? Why and tis for faſhions ſake that we arreſt you. Whoſe that Sir? Oh, In Eſſex! I thought you had beene in London, where now your buſines lyes, honeſtye from Eſſex will be a great while a comming ſir, you ſhould looke out an honeſt paire of Cittizens. No, there's enow in Towne. To him then lets ſet forward:—Yeoman Spider man, caſtan eye about for Maiſter Blaſtfield. Can you blame him ſir—we that dayly fray away Knight's, may fright away Boyes I hope. Bleſſe maiſter Quomodo. Verie true ſir,—but this Gentleman lighting into our hands firſt— Wee thought good to make vſe of that oportunitie, and hold him faſt. So we told him ſir, and that it lay in your worſhips curtezie to arreſt which you pleaſe. Do you heere ſir, a my troth we pittie you, ha you a ny ſtore of Crownes about you? I muſt tell you this, you haue fell in to the hands of a moſt mercileſſe deuourer, the verie gul athe citie, ſhould you offer him mony, Goods or lands now, hee'd rather haue your bodie in priſon, hee's a ſuch a nature. Eaſ. Priſon w'are vn don then. Hee's a ſuch a nature, looke?—Let him owe any man a ſpite • what's his courſe: he will lend him mony to day, a purpoſe to reſt him tomorrow. Has at leaſt ſixteene at this inſtant proceeded in both the Counters: ſome batchler, ſome maſters, ſome doctors of captiuitie of 20. years ſtanding and he deſires nothing more then impriſonment. I, then things would not bee as they are—what will you ſay to vs if wee procure you two ſubſtantiall ſubſi die Cittizens to baile you ſpite on's heart, and ſet you at li bertie to finde out maiſter Blaſtfield. Much. I loue to preuent the malice of ſuch a raſcall, perhaps you might find maiſter Blaſtfield to night. Fie.—and youle ſeeke to ſecure your baile, becauſe they will be two Cittizens of good account, you muſt doe that for your credit ſake. A pox on him, you cut his throte then,—no words. I told you ſo. Vnder your leaue maſter Quomodo, the Gentleman craues the furtherance of an houre, and it ſorts well with our occaſion at this time, hauing a little vrgent buſines at Guild hall, at which minute weele returne, and ſee what agreement is made. Hee's your priſoner; and being ſafe in your houſe at your owne diſpoſing, you cannot denie him ſuch a requeſt: beſide, he hath a little faith in Ma. Blaſtfields comming ſir. Are you the Gentleman in diſtreſſe? Oh 〈◊〉 • ou mercie tis Blaſtfield indeede. That's all your refuge. Gentleman, what's your to • her name? O Maiſter Eaſie—I would we could rather plea ſure you otherwiſe Maiſter Eaſie, you ſhould ſoone perceiue it, ile ſpeake a proud word we haue pittied more Gentlemen in diſtreſſe, then any two Cittizens within the freedome— but to be baile to ſea • en hundred pound action, is a matter of ſhroud weight. Shall we venture once agen, that haue beene ſo of ten vndone by Gentlemen? I like the Gentlemans face well, hee doe's not looke as if he would deceiue vs. Come weele make a deſperate voyage once agen, weele trye his honeſtie, and take his ſingle bond, of body Goods and Lands. Maiſter Quomodo? Come then, and be a witneſſe to a Re • ulliſance. Maiſter Eaſie, you muſt haue an eſpeciall care now to find out that Blaſtfield. The 〈◊〉 will 〈…〉 you ſelſe, Maiſter Quomodo will come vpon vt, and 〈◊〉 you. Well ſince I ſee you haue ſuch a good minde to bee ho neſt • e lea • e ſome greater 〈…〉 ſweate with you to finde him my ſelfe. Where ſhall we ſeeke him now? you leade me fayre • aunt's ſir. A Cittizen of my e • ſe and ſubſtance to walke ſo long a foote. How would you had me hold him by the tayle ſir then? I am glad, I am where I am then, I perceiue twas time of all handes. What? haue you found him yet? neither? what's to be done now? ile venter my bodie no further for any Gentle mans pleaſure, I know not how ſoone I may be cald vppon, and now to ouer-heate my ſelfe.— This is you that ſlept with him, you can make fooles of vs, but ile turne you ouer to Quomodo fort. Ile preuent mine owne danger. Tho I loue Gentlemen well, I doe not meane to bee vndone for 'em. Made fooles of vs! not to be found! Gentlemen, S'lid they were borne to vndo vs I think, but for my part, Ile make an oath before maiſter Qomodo here, nere to doe Gentlemen good while I liue. Away; if you had any grace in you, you would bee a ſhamed to looke vs ith face, ywis I wonder with what browe you can come amongſt vs, I ſhould ſeeke my fortunes fa • re enough if I were you, and neither returne to Eſſex, to bee a ſhame to my predeceſſors, nor remaine about London, to be a mocke to my ſucceſſors. Here are his lands forfeyted to vs maſter Quomodo, and to auoyd the inconſcionable trouble of law, all the aſſi • • ance he made to vs, we willingly reſigne to you. But maſter Quomodo, if you would but conceyue it aright, the land would fall fitter to you then to vs. You haue a towardly ſonne and heyre as we heare. We haue neither poſteritie in Towne nor hope for any abroad; we haue wiues, but the markes haue beene out of their mouths theſe twentie yeares, and as it appeares, they did little good when they were in: wee could not ſtande a bout it ſir, to g • t riches and children too ▪ tis more then one man can doe. And I am of thoſe Citizens mindes that ſay, let our wi • es make ſhift for children and they will, they get none of vs; and I cannot thinke, but he that has both much wealth and many children, has had more helpes comming in then himſelfe. Tis ſo aſſurde vnto you. Landed maiſter Quomodo. The happyeſt good that euer Shortyard felt, I want to be expreſt, my mirth is ſuch, To bee ſtruck now eene when his ioyes were hye, Men onely kiſſe their knaueries, and ſo dye, Iu'e often markt it. Hee was a famous Coozner while he liu'd, And now his Sonne ſhall reape it, ile ha the lands, Let him Studye law after, tis no labour to vndoe him for euer: but for Eaſie, Onely good confidence did make him fooliſh, And not the lack of Sence, that was not it, Tis worldly craft beates downe a Schollars wit, For this our Sonne and heyre now, hee From his conception was entayl'd an Aſſe, And hee ha's kept it well, twentie fiue yeares now, Then the ſleighteſt art will doo't, the landes lye faire, No Sinne to begger a deceiuers heyre. I heare you ſir. Holde, holde. Why doe but heare me ſir, you will not thinke what I haue done for you. Why looke you, tis not ſo, your not tolde true, I haue Cooſned him agen meerely for you, Meerely for you ſir, twas my meaning then That you ſhould wed her, and haue all agen. A my troth 'its true ſir: looke you then heere ſir, you ſhall not miſſe a little ſcrowle ſir, pray ſir, let not the Cittie knowe me for a knaue, there be ritcher men would enuie my prefer ment if I ſhould be knowne before e'm. How now? freſh warders. This is the fruite of Craft, Like him that ſhootes vp hye, lookes for the ſhaft And findes it in his fore-head, ſo does hit The Arrowe of our fate, wit deſtroyes wit: The head the bodyes bane, and his owne beares, You hae Corne enough, you neede not reape mine eares, Sweete Maiſter Blaſtfield. My Lord ile quickly reſolue you that it comes to me This couſner whom too long I call'd my patrone, To my thought dying, and the foole his ſonne Poſſeſt of all, which my braine partly ſweat for, I held it my beſt vertue, by a plot To get from him what for him was ill got. When no ſooner mine, But I was glad more quickly to reſigne. Hence foorth no woman ſhall complaine for meaſure.
speeches.Sale:: Oh, they are bils for Chambers. Why here's vertue ſtill; I like that thing that's neceſ ſary, as well as pleaſant. Whoſe tis? in the name of the blacke Angels, An dro Gruill. Lethe? Not hither. But do's he paſſe for Lethe. Has ſpyed vs ore his paper. Maſter Lethe! Why we ſupt with you laſt night ſir! Not yet! The horne were a fit place. Waſt it. The horne. I, the feinds in't, you're patient, you put vp all. Deuils.
speeches.Rerra:: Ha? ſeeke you for newes, there's for you!
speeches.Lathe:: Gentlemen your pardon, I remember you not.
speeches.Lethe:: Oh cry you mercy, 'tis ſo long agoe, I had quite forgot you, I muſt be forgiuen, Acquaintaince, deere ſocietie, ſuites and things, Do ſo flowe to mee; that had I not the better memorie! Twould be a wonder I ſhould know my ſelfe, Eſteeme is made of ſuch a dizzy mettall; I haue receiu'd of many gifts ore night Whome I haue forgot ere morning, meeting the men, I wiſht em to remember me agen, They doo ſo: then if I forget agen, I know what helpt before, that will helpe then, This is my courſe, for memorie I haue been told Twentie preſerues, the beſt I find is gold; Ey truely! are you not knights yet, Gentlemen.
speeches.Leth:: No, that muſt bee lookt into, tis your owne ſault, I haue ſome ſtore of Veniſon, where ſhall we deuoure it, Gentlemen? For Veniſon, fit, The horne hauing chaſt it, At the horne—weele Rime to that.— Thats the true rime indeed, wee hunt our Veniſon twice I tell you, firſt out a'th parke, next out a'th Bellie. Right. I pray doo ſo. Eaſily remembred that you know! Then I muſt proudly venture it; to me good wo man. Prethe be breife then. I know a gallant Gentleman of the name, one maſ ter Andro Gruill and well receiude amongſt Ladyes. Good woman if he be a Gruill, hee's a Gentleman i'th mornings: thats a Gentleman a'th firſt, you canot tel me O my teeth. Kitchin, puh, fah. Oh let mee not indure her! Knowe you not mee good woman? Good, ſhee knowes me not, my glory do's diſquire mee, Beſide my poorer name being drencht in Lethe, Sheele hardly vnderſtand me, what a freſh ayre can doo! I may employ her as a priuate drudge, To paſſe my letters and ſecure my luſt, And nere be noted mine, to ſhame my blood, And drop my ſtayning birth vppon my raiment, faith good woman you will hardly get to the ſpeech of maſter Andro, I tell you. You muſt take heed how you ſpeak ill of him now I cantell you; hee's ſo employde. For his behauiour, wiſdome, and other vertues. Hee's the better regarded for that amongſt Courti ers, for thats but a needy qualitie! In pitty of thy long iourney, there's ſix-pence Britiſh: tend vpon me, I haue buſines for you. Two pole off at leaſt. It goes not by cleannes here good woman, if you were fowler, ſo you were brauer, you might come neerer. You ſee I'me patient gentlemen ▪
speeches.Moth:: By your leaue and like your worſhip. I beſeech one word with your worſhip. Pray can your worſhip tell me any tydings of one Andro Gruill, a poore ſonne of mine owne. That not he then! Hee is no Gentleman that I meane. No truely, his father was an honeſt vpright Tooth-drawer. An't pleaſe your worſhip, I haue made a fore iour ney out, all this vacant time, to come vp and ſee my ſonne Andro, poore Walter Gruill his Father has layd his life, and left mee a lone woman, I haue not one husband in all the world, therefore my comming vp is for reliefe an't like your worſhip, hoping that my ſonne Andro is in ſome place about the Kitchin.
speeches.Mo:: Or a ſeruingman to ſome Kinght of worſhip. Alaſſe, an't pleeaſe your worſhip, I neuer ſawe ſuch a glorious ſuite ſince the hower I was • erſend. No? Marry hang him, and like your Worſhip, I haue knowen the day when no body carde to ſpeake to him! Imployde for what? His vertues? no tis well knowen, his father was too poore a man to bring him vp to any vertues; hee can ſcarce write and reade. If it be ſo, then heele be great ſhortly, for he has no good parts about him. Alack the day, I know your worſhip ſcornes to cal me mother: tis not a thing fit for your worſhip indeede, ſuch a ſimple old woman as I am. Ile waite vpon your Worſhip. I am a cleane ould woman, an't like your Worſhip. Nay and that be the faſhion, I hope I ſhall (Exit. get it ſhortly, there's no woman ſo ould but ſhe may learne; and as an old Lady delights in a young Page or monckey, ſo there are young Courtiers will be hungry vpon an old wo man, I warrant you.
Well good woman, or mother, or what you will. Ah ſir, I came not hither but to win. Hee's baſe that viſits not his friends: It is a thing in vſe and euer was, I paſſe this time. Tut, the Dice are ours, Then wonder not at thoſe that haue moſt powrs ▪ Are theſe they? Welcome deere Angels, where y'are curſt nere ſtay. Dick, Hell-gill: the hapie Newes. Peace, what is ſhe? Of what parentage? Is ſhe wife or maide? Ide rather ſhee'd beene a wife. Oh Adulterie is a great deale ſweeter in my minde. That will moue well. Wee're for you. Preſent her with this Iewell my firſt token. Come gallants, ile bring you to a Beauty ſhal ſtricke your eyes into your hearts, what you ſee you ſhall deſire, yet neuer enioy. No more of my credit, and a Gentlewoman of a great houſe, Noble parentage, vnmatchable Education, my plain Pung. I may, grace her with the name of a Curtizan, a Back ſlider, a Proſtitution, or ſuch a Toy, but when all comes • o al tis but a plaine Pung, looke you Gentlemen, that's ſhe, be holde her. La you now—you ſhall not ſay ile be proud to you Gentlemen, I giue you leaue to ſalute her ▪ I me afraide of nothing now, but that ſheele vtterlie diſgrace e'm, turn taile to e'm, and place their kiſſes behinde her, no by my faith, ſhe deceiues me, by my troth ſha's kiſt am both with her lips: I thanke you for that muſick maiſters, ſli'd they both court her at once, and ſee if ſhe ha not the wit to ſtand ſtill and let e'm: I thinke if two men were brewde into one, there is that wo man would drink e'm vp both. Nay, he are you me Gentlemen. This is good yfaith, indure this and be a ſlaue fore uer, ſince you neither ſauour of good breeding nor bringing vp, Ile ſlice your hamſtrings but ile make you ſhow man nerly—pox on you, leaue courting, I ha not the heart to hurt an Engliſhman yfaith, or elſe— Prethee lets be merrie, nothing elſe—heere, fetch ſome wine. Maiſter Blaſtfield and Maiſter Eaſie, y'are kinde Gentlemen both. I • nuyfed e'm hyther to looke vpon her, brought e'm along with me, gaue e'm leaue to ſalute her in kindnes, what doe they but moſte ſawcilie fall in loue with her, verye impudently court her for themſelues, and like two craftye Atturneyes, finding a hole in my leaſe, goe about to defeate me of my right. The moſte vnciuilſt part that you haue ſeene, I know theile be ſorry for't when they haue done, for ther's no man but giues a ſigh after his ſin of women, I knowe it by my ſelfe. Now ſome good newes yet to recouer my Repute, and grace me in this company; Gentlemen, are we friendes among our ſelues? Then heere comes Reuiſh to confirme our Amitie— Wag ▪ taile, ſalute • hem all they are friendes. The Father does elect me for the man, The Daughter ſayes the ſame. You may beleeue it ſir, now what ſayes her anſwere? How? Drudge, peace, or— Horror, horror, i'me ſmother'd, let me goe, torment me not. What's your name ſir?—O crie you mercie maſter Eaſie. Blaſtfield's an Aſſe, I haue ſought him theſe two dayes to beate him. I, and three more.— No in truth. O vilde ſlaue! Oh intollerable! I beſeech your good Lordſhip if I muſt haue an outward pu niſhment, let me not marrie an inward, whoſe laſtes will nere out, but growe worſe and worſe: I haue a wife ſtaies for me this morning with ſeauen hundred pound in her purſſe, let me be ſpeedily whipt and be gone, I beſeech your Lord ſhip. I was betrayed, yes faith. O good my Lord. Who ſhould that be? Or who would doote, that has beene ſo abuſde? A troubleſome pennance—ſir. Maiſter Eaſie. Maiſter Quomodo. Maſſe I forget my mother all this while, Ile make her doo't at firſt, pray mother your bleſſing for once. Call me ſlaue as much as you will, but doe not ſhame me now, let the world knowe you are my Mother. You would not beleeue me Mother.
speeches.Pand:: Come, leaue your puling and ſighing. Why? to thy better aduancement, wouldſt thou a pretty beautifull—Iuicy ſquall, liue in a poore thrumbd houſe i'th cun try in ſuch ſeruile—habiliments, and may well paſſe for a gentle woman i'th Citie, do's not 5 hundred do ſo thinkst thou, and with worſe faces, oh, now in theſe latter dayes, the Deuill raygning tis an age for clouen creatures? but why ſad now? yet indeed tis the faſhion of any Curtizan to be ſea-ſicke i'th firſt Voyage, but at next ſhee proclaimes open wars, like a beaten ſouldier: why Nor thampton-ſhire Laſſe do'ſt dreame of virginity now? remember a looſe-bodied Gowne wench, & let it goe, wires, & tyres, bents and bums, felts and falls, thou that ſhalt deceiue the world, that Gentle women indeed ſhall not be knowen from others; I haue a maſter to whome I muſt prefer thee, after the aforeſayd decking, Lethe by name, a man of one moſt admired property, he can both loue thee and for thy better aduancement be thy Pandar himſelfe, an ex lent ſparke of humility. Why I doe acknowledge it, and I thinke I doe you a pleaſure in't. Bound? nay and you proue a harlot, youle be looſe ynough. Nay thats certain, nor a 1000. more of you, I know, you are all chaſt ynough, till one thing or other tempt you • deny a Sattin gowne and you dare now? True they will not, moſt diſſembler. Why, therfore take heart, faint not at all, Women nere riſe, but when they fall, Let a man breake, hee's gone, blowen vp, A womans breaking ſets her vp, Virginitie is no Citie—Trade, You're out a'th Freedome, when you're a mayde, Downe with the lattis tis but thin, Let courser beauties worke within: Whome the light mocks, thou art faire and freſh, The guilded flies, will light vpon thy fleſh.
speeches.Count:: Beſhrew you now, why did you entice me from my father Well heauen forgiue you, you traine me vp too't. And if I ſhould proue a harlot now, I ſhould be bound to curſe you. If I had not a deſire to goe like a gentlewoman, you ſhould be hangd, ere you ſhould get me too't I warrant you. You knowe I haue no power to doo't, and that makes you ſo wilfull: for what woman is there ſuch a beaſt that will deny any thing that is good. No, and ſhee beare a braue mind ſhee will not I warrant you. Beſhrew your ſweet enchantments, you have wun. Oh as ſoone as may be, I am in a ſwone till I bee a gentlewoman, and you know what fleſh is mans meate, tell it be dreſt.
speeches.Pan:: How eaſily ſoft women are vndone: So farewell holeſome weeds where treaſure pants, And welcome ſilkes, where lyes diſeaſe and wants: Come wench, now flow thy Fortunes in to bleſſe thee, Ile bring thee where thou ſhalt be taught to dreſſe thee! Moſt certain, no more a woman.
An vnfortunate one ſir. I ſhall keepe Chriſtmaſſe with him ſit, where your health ſhall likewiſe vndoubtedly be remembred, and there vpon I pledge you:—I would ſue for your name ſir. Kind maiſter Blaſtfield, your deerer acquaintance. Faith I'me ſcatterd. Sir you binde me infinitely in theſe courteſies. I'me glad you tell me that yet, then I',e indifferent. Well, come: who throwes? I ſet all theſe. Lets ſearch him Gentlemen, I think he wears a ſmock: No, how did he for the Reſt? Twas a prettie ſhift yfaith. A miſchiefe on't to looſe all: I could— Twas al I brought vp with me, I proteſt maſter Blaſt ſield, all my rent till next quarter. It ſeemes y'are wel knowne maſter Blaſtfield, and your credite verie ſpacious here ith Citie. So readily ſir. Nay ile forſweare dicing. Nay I was but in ieſt ſir. Ha, ha ha. Troth, and you ha reaſon to thanke him ſir, t'was a verie friendly anſwere. I promiſe you ſir I admire your carriage, and begin to hold a mor reu'rend reſpect of you. Send to Maſter Goome, or Maſter Profit, the Mer cer and Goldſmith. Not I ſir, by no meanes: maſter Blaſtfield knowes I'me further in want then himſelfe, my hope reſts all vpon him, it ſtands vpon the loſſe of my credit to Night, if I walke with out money. As nere as can be yfaith. Tis moſt certaine maſter Quomodo. Nay, neuer vex your ſelfe ſweet maſter Blaſtfield. A little ſir. Why la! by my troth t' was kindly ſpoken. Nay, maiſter Blaſtfield, you doe not heare what ma ſter Quomodo ſaid ſince, like an honeſt true Citizen yfaith: rather then you ſhould grow diſeaſde vpon't, you ſhall take vp a commoditie of two hundred pounds • orth of cloath. Nay, Ile ſay that, it comes in as fit a time as can be. Oh horrible, are there ſuch fool • s in towne? Nay be perſwaded in that maſter Blaſtfield tis readie money at, the 〈◊〉 beſide, the 〈◊〉 and all falls in as pa • as can be 〈◊〉 helpe it. Right yfaith. Pox on't. I forgot all this: what meant I to • wagger before I had money in my purſe? how do's maiſter Quomodo? is the Bond readie? Come we muſt be friends, heer's my hand. Is it your cuſtome to returne ſo ſoone ſir? How the poore raskall's all in a froth? Tis true yfaith, they beare men and money, and that's the world. I beſeech you ſir. Nay pray maſter Blaſtfield. What doe you meane ſir? By my troth you doe your ſelfe wrong tho maiſter Blaſtfield. But to auoid ſtrife, you ſhall haue your will of mee for once. How like you my Roman hand yfaith? Ile mend that preſently. Why Maiſter Blaſtfield? If he want twentie on't lets take it. Is That your wife maiſter Quomodo? Vnder your leaue ſir, ile ſhow my ſelfe a Gentle man. You teach me the beſt law Lady. A very good grace to make a Lawyer. Fye, fie. A match. Did I not tell you ſtill he would. Nay y'are no leſſe Maiſter Blaſtfield, looke too't, by my troth, I muſt needes confeſſe ſir, you ha bene vncommon ly kinde to me, ſince I ha beene in Towne, but maiſter Alſup ſhall know on't. I beſeech you ſir. Stay, this is Lethes haunt, ſee, we haue catcht him. Come, are you not to blame—not to giue place?— To vs I meane— And then indeede ſhe turnes her backe to ſome man liuing. They'r worth golde Maiſter Blaſtfield. Boy. Where left you Maiſter Blaſtfield your maiſter, ſay you? Methinks I haue noe beeing without his companie tis ſo full of kindenes and delight, I holde him to be the one ly Companyon in earth.
